lessons.title: Getting paid at least the minimum
lessons.html:
Alberta’s Employment Standards Code sets minimum standards that employers must provide to employees. This lesson is for people who are paid to work, not for people who are writing payroll rules.

As of 10 November 2026 (America/Regina), Alberta’s minimum-wage page said employers must pay at least the minimum wage. The general minimum wage for most employees was $15 an hour. A lower student rate of $13 an hour can apply to students under 18, with restrictions. Separate weekly or monthly minimums apply to some salespersons and to some domestic employees. Wages do not include tips or expense money.

Employers must also follow payment-of-earnings rules. They must pay at least once a month, or on a daily, weekly, bi-weekly, or semi-monthly pay period. They must pay you within 10 consecutive days after the end of the pay period, unless employment has ended. You must be paid in Canadian currency, by cash, cheque, or direct deposit into an account of your choice. You are not considered paid until you have received the funds.

At the end of each pay period, your employer must give you a statement of earnings. That statement should show the period, regular and overtime hours, wage and overtime rates, each kind of earning listed separately (such as wages, overtime, general holiday pay, and vacation pay), deductions and the reason for each one, and any hours taken off instead of overtime.

These figures can change. Check the live pages before you rely on a number.

lessons.title: Overtime hours and overtime pay
lessons.html:
Hours of work matter for what you are owed. Daily maximums, rest breaks, and days of rest are set out on Alberta’s “Hours of work and rest” page. Another Range Path course already maps those rest-and-break rules for people who supervise. This lesson does not repeat that list. If you need breaks or a weekly day of rest, read the live hours page.

This lesson covers overtime, which that other course did not teach.

As of 10 November 2026 (America/Regina), Alberta’s overtime page said overtime is all hours worked over 8 hours a day or 44 hours a week, whichever is greater. That is called the 8/44 rule. Most employees, including people paid a salary, are entitled to overtime pay. There are exemptions for some industries and professions — check the live page rather than guessing.

Except where there is a written overtime agreement, an employer must pay overtime of at least 1.5 times your regular wage rate for overtime hours. Instead of paying that money, an employer may give time off with pay (banked overtime) at a rate of at least one hour off for each overtime hour, but only as part of an overtime agreement. Banked time must usually be used within 6 months of the end of the pay period in which you earned it, unless a collective agreement says otherwise.

Employers and employees cannot make an agreement that pays less than the Code’s minimum overtime. If your workplace uses an averaging arrangement or is in an industry with different overtime rules, read those pages before you do the math.

lessons.title: Vacation and general holidays
lessons.html:
Most employees — full-time and part-time — are entitled to vacation time and vacation pay. As of 10 November 2026 (America/Regina), Alberta’s vacation page said you must usually work for one year before you are entitled to vacation time. After that, the minimums are:

  • 2 weeks with pay after each of the first 4 years of employment
  • 3 weeks with pay after 5 consecutive years of employment

For people paid hourly, weekly, or by commission, vacation pay is generally 4% of wages for the 2-week entitlement and 6% after 5 years. If employment ends before 12 months, the employer must pay 4% of the wages you earned. Time on a job-protected leave counts toward your length of employment for vacation.

Employers must give vacation, and employees must take it. It should be one unbroken period unless you ask in writing to split it. If you cannot agree on dates, the employer can decide, but must give at least 2 weeks’ written notice of the start date.

Alberta has 9 general holidays, also called statutory holidays: New Year’s Day, Alberta Family Day, Good Friday, Victoria Day, Canada Day, Labour Day, Thanksgiving Day, Remembrance Day, and Christmas Day. Employers may choose to recognize extra days, such as Heritage Day or the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

You are generally eligible for general holiday pay if you have worked for the same employer for at least 30 workdays in the 12 months before the holiday. What you are owed then depends on whether the holiday is a regular day of work for you and whether you work that day. The official page explains those calculations. This course does not walk through every formula.

Alberta has 9 general holidays, and employers may recognize additional days.

lessons.title: Job-protected leaves and ending employment
lessons.html:
Job-protected leaves give you time off to deal with life events without losing your job. As of 10 November 2026 (America/Regina), Alberta said employees are eligible for most of these leaves after 90 days with the same employer. The leaves are unpaid, though Employment Insurance may provide income support in some cases.

Alberta lists leaves such as bereavement, compassionate care, critical illness, domestic violence, long-term illness and injury, maternity and parental leave, personal and family responsibility, and others. Each leave has its own length and notice rules. Read the page for the leave that applies to you before you give notice.

Ending a job also has written-notice rules. Notice is not required if employment is 90 days or less. If you resign after that, you must usually give 1 week of written notice if you have worked less than 2 years, or 2 weeks if you have worked 2 years or more.

If the employer ends the job — and it is not just cause or another listed exception — written notice grows with your service: 1 week (more than 90 days but less than 2 years), 2 weeks (2 to less than 4 years), 4 weeks (4 to less than 6), 5 weeks (6 to less than 8), 6 weeks (8 to less than 10), or 8 weeks (10 years or more). The employer may pay termination pay instead of notice, or use a mix of both.

During a notice period, the employer cannot reduce your earnings or require you to use vacation or banked overtime. Final earnings must be paid within 10 calendar days after the end of the pay period in which the job ended, or 31 calendar days after your last day. This course does not advise anyone on dismissing a person or on common-law severance.

quiz.prompt: Most job-protected leaves are available after 90 days with the same employer and are unpaid.
Notice is not required when employment has lasted 90 days or less.
After 10 years of service, the employer notice period on the official table is 8 weeks (unless an exception applies).
This course tells an employer how to dismiss someone for just cause.

lessons.title: How to make an employment standards complaint
lessons.html:
If you think your employer is not following the Employment Standards Code, you can make a complaint. Talk to your employer first. Alberta says that is the first step in trying to resolve the issue.

You may complain while you are still employed, or at any time up to 6 months after your last day of employment. Complaints can be submitted online at no cost. They must be truthful. Your employer cannot terminate your employment because you make, or are about to make, a complaint.

A formal complaint can lead to pay you are owed or to other issues being resolved. Your name will be associated with the complaint and shared with the employer. That is different from an anonymous tip, which does not use your name and will not update you on the result.

Employment Standards can look at issues the Code covers, such as wages, overtime, minimum wage, vacation, general holiday pay, pay statements, unauthorized deductions, hours of work and rest, job-protected leaves, and termination. It does not handle Records of Employment, Employment Insurance, occupational health and safety, WCB claims, human-rights complaints, or tax deductions. Those belong to other offices.

Before you start, wait one pay period if the issue is about wages or other earnings, in case the next pay statement fixes it. Waiting is not required for urgent matters such as job-protected leaves. Gather documents that help, such as your wage, the employer’s address, two ways to contact you, timesheets, and your employment contract if you have one.

You need an Alberta.ca Account to submit the online complaint. Work must have been performed in Alberta, in a provincially regulated industry, by an employee (not a contractor). If you are in a union, issues are often handled through a grievance, not this complaint.

quiz.prompt: Talking with your employer is the first step before submitting a complaint.
You may file a complaint while you still work there, or up to 6 months after your last day.
There is no cost to submit an employment standards complaint online.
An employer may fire you because you are about to make an employment standards complaint.

keptBack.sourceDisclaimer: This course is general information for workers about Alberta employment standards, based on official Government of Alberta pages. It is not legal advice, not an HR course, and not a guide for supervisors on how to hire, discipline, or dismiss someone. Rules can change, and some jobs have exceptions. If a page differs from the legislation, Alberta says the legislation is considered correct. Always check the live official page, and get help from Alberta Employment Standards or a qualified advisor if you have a real workplace problem.
